review.summary: healthy. Tests: 25 passed, link checker bad 0. Arithmetic in 1.6, 2.1, 4.6, 6.1, 6.4, 6.5, 7.4 checks out. Top findings: (1) 8.1's worker semaphore is module-level, so it caps workers across every concurrent orchestrator run, not "one per run" as the comment and PR20-3-F3 say. (2) 8.3's fan-in claims to merge 8.1's six-site run, but its quorum counts only site-scope findings, so 8.1's single cluster-scope W2 worker would file no fleet ticket. (3) Seven glossary entries still say "Day N", which STYLE.md forbids.

findings.checklist_item: Plain language: code stays as code, with text that says what it does
findings.title: 8.1 worker semaphore is module-level, so it caps workers across all runs, not per run
findings.claim: The comment says `SLOTS` is "one per orchestrator run", and the prose says the semaphore "holds the run to four". But `SLOTS = asyncio.Semaphore(4)` is created at module level, outside any run. The 5.6 worked answer runs the nightly batch with 8 concurrent orchestrator runs (week-05 line 848); with this code they would share one semaphore and the whole batch would run at most 4 workers, not 4 per run. Readers copying the sketch get a different throughput than the text promises.
findings.evidence: weeks/week-08-multi-agent-systems.md:91 `SLOTS = asyncio.Semaphore(4)         # one per orchestrator run, shared by every spawn call`, defined next to `WORKER_SPEC` at module scope; `run_worker` and `spawn_workers` close over it. Decision PR20-3-F3 describes it as 'one per orchestrator run'.
findings.proposed_change: Either create the semaphore inside the orchestrator run (for example `st.slots = asyncio.Semaphore(4)` in the run's state, passed to `run_worker`) and keep the comment, or keep it module-level and change the comment and prose to 'one per process: caps workers across every run in the batch'. Test: start two orchestrator runs concurrently with stub workers that sleep 0.2 s and assert the peak concurrent worker count (8 for per-run, 4 for per-process).

findings.checklist_item: Flow: join lessons so it reads as a story; simplifying must not change meaning
findings.title: 8.3 fan-in is said to merge 8.1's run, but its quorum ignores 8.1's cluster-scope W2 finding
findings.claim: Line 436 introduces the code as 'a fan-in for the six-site fixture from 8.1'. In 8.1 the orchestrator spawns one cluster-scope worker for the W2 feed (`scope_id="W2"`, `site=None`; lines 113 and 173). The fan-in's quorum set is `{f.site for f in ok if f.site in W2_SITES ...}` (lines 454–459), so a cluster-scope confirmed finding never votes and 8.1's actual run would file no fleet ticket. The code only works for the one-worker-per-W2-site decomposition (8.3's own Try-it fixture, or 8.1's variant C).
findings.evidence: week-08 line 113: 'T2: spawns two workers. One checks the fleet-level W2 weather feed.' Line 455: `w2 = {f.site for f in ok if f.site in W2_SITES and f.hypothesis == "feed" ...}`; SiteFinding (lines ~158–165) sets `site` only 'when scope is "site"'.
findings.proposed_change: Either change line 436 to 'a fan-in for the one-worker-per-W2-site split (8.1's variant C, and the fixture in Try it below)', or add one branch before the quorum: a cluster-scope finding for (W2, feed) that passes provenance is the fleet verdict on its own, and the site-level quorum applies only when the work was split per site. Add a sentence saying which decomposition the quorum is for. Test: run the fan-in on two stub inputs, one cluster finding and five site findings, and assert a fleet ticket in both cases.

findings.checklist_item: Flow: never refer to "Day N"; refer to the lesson by number, with a link
findings.title: Seven glossary entries still cite "Day N" instead of a lesson number
findings.claim: STYLE.md says never to refer to 'Day N'. The glossary does so in seven entries: Findings vs errors ('the Day 7 null-weather case', line 388), Memory injection ('Day 19's', line 601), Minimal-prompt rule ('the Day 4 discipline', line 622), Overlap tool ('Day 24's finding', line 682), Replanning ('(Day 11)', line 826), Section ablation ('Day 23's result', line 898), Workflow-shaped tool ('Day 3's `get_site_metrics`', line 1159). A phone reader has no way to map a day number to a lesson.
findings.evidence: rg 'Day \d+' glossary.md returns lines 388, 601, 622, 682, 826, 898, 1159. STYLE.md, Flow: 'Never refer to "Day N". Refer to the lesson by number, with a link'.
findings.proposed_change: Replace each with the lesson reference: Day 7 → the Week 1 review; Day 19 → 3.4; Day 4 → 1.4; Day 24 → 4.2; Day 11 → 2.3; Day 23 → 4.1; Day 3 → 1.3, each as a link in the glossary's existing style. Test: `rg 'Day \d+' glossary.md` returns nothing; `python -m pytest -q` still passes.

findings.checklist_item: Plain language: simplifying must not change meaning
findings.title: 8.3 note's conflict example reads as two different sites, which the example text says is not a conflict
findings.claim: The 2026-11-01 note defines a conflict as 'two different verdicts within one (scope, hypothesis) group, for example one site's feed finding *confirmed* and another *rejected*'. 'Another' most naturally means another site's finding. But site findings carry `scope_id` = the site, so two sites are two groups, and the example text (line ~462) says 'A W2 site that simply rejects the feed hypothesis is not a conflict; it just doesn't vote yes.' The example in the note therefore contradicts the body unless 'another' means a second finding for the same site.
findings.evidence: week-08 line 511 vs the paragraph after the code block: 'A conflict is the same site giving two verdicts on one hypothesis... A W2 site that simply rejects the feed hypothesis is not a conflict.' Decision PR20-2-F3 reason: 'confirmed vs rejected on the feed hypothesis'.
findings.proposed_change: Reword the example to: 'for example two findings for the same site on the feed hypothesis, one *confirmed* and one *rejected*. A different site rejecting the feed hypothesis is a separate group and simply does not vote yes.'

findings.checklist_item: Accuracy: arithmetic and counts in the text
findings.title: 6.4 quotes a ±25-point CI from a 1.96 multiplier while 6.5 and the quiz use t = 2.36 for the same 8 tasks
findings.claim: With SE ≈ 0.13 (correct: SD 0.356/√8 = 0.126), the stated '95% confidence interval is roughly ±25 points' uses the normal 1.96 multiplier. Lesson 6.5 (line 709) and the Week 6 self-quiz answer 4 (line 900) use the t multiplier 2.36 for 7 degrees of freedom on the same 8-task design, which gives ±0.30. A reader comparing the two lessons sees two different CI widths for the same sample size and cannot tell which rule to apply.
findings.proposed_change: Change line 601 to 'The 95% confidence interval is roughly ±30 points (t with 7 degrees of freedom, the multiplier 6.5 uses)'. Alternatively keep ±25 and add '(using 1.96; with the t multiplier from 6.5 it is ±30)'. No test; recompute by hand.

findings.checklist_item: Files: glossary.md — terms, alphabetical, each pointing to the lesson that introduces it
findings.title: Glossary has a duplicate Super-step entry and τ²-bench filed under B
findings.claim: Two entries define the same LangGraph term with different pointers: 'Super-step' (line 981, points to 3.5) and 'Superstep (LangGraph)' (line 984, points to 8.3). The glossary's own rule is one entry per term pointing to the lesson that introduces it; the Orchestrator–worker entry shows the pattern for a term that two lessons extend. Separately, 'τ²-bench' sits under B (line 117, between 'Batch-level deadline' and 'Binary / weighted / hybrid scoring'), where no reader will look for it.
findings.evidence: glossary.md lines 981 '**Super-step**' and 984 '**Superstep (LangGraph)**'; line 117 '**τ²-bench**' inside the '## B' section.
findings.proposed_change: Merge the two Super-step entries into one ('Super-step (LangGraph)') that keeps both facts (one checkpoint per super-step; transactional, failed branch applies no updates, successful branches saved) and ends 'See [3.5] and [8.3]'. Move τ²-bench to the end of T (after 'Turn latency') or into the Numbers/symbols group at the top, and add a 'τ-bench' cross-reference if wanted. Test: `python -m pytest -q` (link checker) still reports bad 0.
